results.question: how long do i keep tax records
results.answer:
You must retain business tax records at least as long as the IRS could legally examine them, which is generally the period of limitations that applies to the return or transaction.  
- For most income‑tax returns, keep supporting records for the **3‑year period of limitations** that follows the year the return was filed, because that is the time the IRS may audit or you may amend the return to claim a refund or credit. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)  
- **Employment‑tax records** (payroll, wage statements, etc.) must be kept for **4 years** after the tax becomes due or is paid, whichever is later. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)  
- If you omitted to report more than 25 % of gross income, the limitation period extends to **6 years**.  
- A **fraudulent return** is not limited; keep the records indefinitely.  
- Records that relate to **property** (to compute depreciation, basis, gain or loss on sale) must be kept until the period of limitations expires for the year in which you dispose of that property. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)  
- Copies of filed tax returns should also be retained because they help prepare future returns and can be needed for future amendments. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)  

In summary, keep records for the longer of the specific period required (e.g., 4 years for employment taxes) and the standard 3‑year period for ordinary income‑tax returns, extending to 6 years when large omissions occur, and indefinitely for fraudulent returns or when needed to support asset disposition calculations.

results.question: cash or accrual accounting whats the difference
results.answer:
Cash‑method accounting and accrual‑method accounting are the two basic ways a business can match income and expenses to tax years.  
**Cash method** – You report income in the year you actually receive it (or “constructively” receive it, such as when a debt is cancelled) and you normally deduct expenses in the year you actually pay them. Example from the IRS text: a check received on 30 Dec 2025 that can’t be deposited until 3 Jan 2026 is still counted as income for 2025, because the right to receive was fixed in 2025 [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15).  
**Accrual method** – You report income in the year it is earned, even if payment comes later, and you deduct or capitalize expenses in the year they are incurred, not necessarily when paid. The IRS notes that a computer sold on 28 Dec 2025 but billed in January 2026 and paid in February 2026 must still be included in 2025 income because the right to receive was fixed in 2025 [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15).  

**Key differences**

| Aspect | Cash method | Accrual method |
|--------|-------------|----------------|
| **When income is recognized** | When you receive the money (or constructively receive it) | When you earn it—when the right to receive is fixed and the amount can be reasonably determined |
| **When expenses are deducted** | When you actually pay the expense | When the expense is incurred—when the liability is fixed and economic performance has occurred |
| **Inventory rule** | Generally allowed for owners with no inventory; if inventory is needed, accrual is required | If inventory is needed, you must use accrual for purchases and sales (unless you qualify as a small business taxpayer) |  

The IRS defines the accrual method in detail; it must satisfy the **all‑events test** (all events fixing the liability have occurred and the amount is determinable) and, for expenses, economic performance must have occurred [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16).  

Because cash can be simpler, most small sole‑proprietors without inventory use it, but owners with inventory are required to use the accrual method, or they can qualify as a small business taxpayer and treat inventory as non‑incidental material or supplies [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)[[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16).  

In short, cash accounting ties tax income and expenses to the actual flow of money, while accrual accounting ties them to the economic reality of when income is earned and expenses are incurred. The choice can affect when you owe tax, what deductions you claim, and how your books reflect real‑world business activity.

You must keep your tax records for the duration that the Internal Revenue Code allows you to use them. In practice, that means:

runs.question: cash or accrual accounting whats the difference
runs.answer:
Cash accounting and accrual accounting differ mainly in **when** income and expenses are recorded for tax purposes.

**Cash method**  
- Income is reported in the year it is actually received (even if paid later).  
- Expenses are deducted in the year they are actually paid (even if incurred earlier).  
- Example: If you receive a check on December 30, 2025 but cannot deposit it until January 3, 2026, you still report the $500 as income for 2025 because you “collect” it that year [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15).  

**Accrual method**  
- Income is reported in the year it is earned, when the right to receive it is fixed and the amount can be reasonably determined, even if payment is received later.  
- Expenses are deducted or capitalized in the year they are incurred, regardless of when they are paid.  
- Example: You sell a computer on December 28, 2025, bill the customer in early January 2026 and receive payment in February 2026. Under accrual, you must include the sale in 2025 income because it was earned that year [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15).

The key difference is the timing rule: cash method matches cash flow (receipt/pay), whereas accrual method matches economic activity (earning/incurring) to correctly match income with related expenses. Both methods must be consistently used and clearly show the business’s income [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5).

runs.question: how long do i keep tax records
runs.answer:
You must retain business tax records at least as long as the IRS could legally examine them, which is generally the period of limitations that applies to the return or transaction.  
- For most income‑tax returns, keep supporting records for the **3‑year period of limitations** that follows the year the return was filed, because that is the time the IRS may audit or you may amend the return to claim a refund or credit. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)  
- **Employment‑tax records** (payroll, wage statements, etc.) must be kept for **4 years** after the tax becomes due or is paid, whichever is later. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)  
- If you omitted to report more than 25 % of gross income, the limitation period extends to **6 years**.  
- A **fraudulent return** is not limited; keep the records indefinitely.  
- Records that relate to **property** (to compute depreciation, basis, gain or loss on sale) must be kept until the period of limitations expires for the year in which you dispose of that property. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)  
- Copies of filed tax returns should also be retained because they help prepare future returns and can be needed for future amendments. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)  

In summary, keep records for the longer of the specific period required (e.g., 4 years for employment taxes) and the standard 3‑year period for ordinary income‑tax returns, extending to 6 years when large omissions occur, and indefinitely for fraudulent returns or when needed to support asset disposition calculations.

runs.question: cash or accrual accounting whats the difference
runs.answer:
Cash‑method accounting and accrual‑method accounting are the two basic ways a business can match income and expenses to tax years.  
**Cash method** – You report income in the year you actually receive it (or “constructively” receive it, such as when a debt is cancelled) and you normally deduct expenses in the year you actually pay them. Example from the IRS text: a check received on 30 Dec 2025 that can’t be deposited until 3 Jan 2026 is still counted as income for 2025, because the right to receive was fixed in 2025 [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15).  
**Accrual method** – You report income in the year it is earned, even if payment comes later, and you deduct or capitalize expenses in the year they are incurred, not necessarily when paid. The IRS notes that a computer sold on 28 Dec 2025 but billed in January 2026 and paid in February 2026 must still be included in 2025 income because the right to receive was fixed in 2025 [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15).  

**Key differences**

| Aspect | Cash method | Accrual method |
|--------|-------------|----------------|
| **When income is recognized** | When you receive the money (or constructively receive it) | When you earn it—when the right to receive is fixed and the amount can be reasonably determined |
| **When expenses are deducted** | When you actually pay the expense | When the expense is incurred—when the liability is fixed and economic performance has occurred |
| **Inventory rule** | Generally allowed for owners with no inventory; if inventory is needed, accrual is required | If inventory is needed, you must use accrual for purchases and sales (unless you qualify as a small business taxpayer) |  

The IRS defines the accrual method in detail; it must satisfy the **all‑events test** (all events fixing the liability have occurred and the amount is determinable) and, for expenses, economic performance must have occurred [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16).  

Because cash can be simpler, most small sole‑proprietors without inventory use it, but owners with inventory are required to use the accrual method, or they can qualify as a small business taxpayer and treat inventory as non‑incidental material or supplies [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)[[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16).  

In short, cash accounting ties tax income and expenses to the actual flow of money, while accrual accounting ties them to the economic reality of when income is earned and expenses are incurred. The choice can affect when you owe tax, what deductions you claim, and how your books reflect real‑world business activity.
